metadata.title: Stacking: An ensemble learning approach to predict student performance in pisa 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 student questionnaire data and achievement outcomes (reading, mathematics, science) for 80 participating countries, but it does not report applying PISA sampling/survey weights or any replicate-weight scheme. The authors describe splitting each country dataset into training/validation/test partitions and optimizing hyperparameters via fivefold cross-validation, which is consistent with standard ML workflows but does not specify complex-survey variance estimation. Because the manuscript does not mention weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) or replicate methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), it is unclear whether population-representative weighting was used; the safest interpretation is that weights were not incorporated into the ML fitting. For analysts wishing to reproduce or extend the work, the PISA technical documentation should be consulted to identify the appropriate student weight and replicate weights, and to decide whether to use weight-aware estimation or design-based evaluation when comparing country-level errors.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that it did not impute missing observations (it converts specific response codes to NaN and then uses base learners “without imputing any missing observations”), so a conventional missing-data handling label is not clearly documented in terms of deletion vs. model-internal missing handling. Because the authors also claim stacking can handle missing data and do not provide a formal rule (e.g., listwise deletion of rows with NaNs, or explicit use of algorithms’ built-in missing-value routing), the exact missing-data strategy is ambiguous. This is a reporting gap for reproducibility, especially given that PISA datasets typically contain nontrivial item nonresponse.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 data for all countries participating in the administration (80 countries). For each subject area (mathematics, reading, science), the authors created a separate dataset by removing irrelevant variables (student/school IDs, birth-month, country-specific items, variables not subject-specific) and variables with 100% missing values. During preparation, response codes for “valid skip,” “not applicable,” “invalid,” and “no response” were converted to NaN (missing). The analysis was conducted separately for each country, and for each country dataset the data were split into training/testing for stacking (80%/20%) and training/validation/testing for blending (60%/20%/20%).

main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement prediction error (MAPE/MAE/MSE/RMSE across PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Stacking produced the lowest mean MAPE for 72/80 countries (90.00%), lowest mean MAE for 74/80 (92.50%), and lowest mean MSE for 75/80 (93.75%). Robust linear mixed-effects models (reference=Stacking) indicated significantly higher errors for XGBoost, HGB, LightGBM, and Blending vs. Stacking for MAPE/MAE/MSE (e.g., MAPE: XGBoost t=13.79, HGB t=13.76, LightGBM t=12.63, Blending t=23.22).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics the study leveraged an ensemble stacking meta-model (with ridge regression as the level-1 learner) to predict mathematics achievement across plausible values, finding that stacking achieved the lowest error metrics for the vast majority of countries (e.g., lowest mean MAPE in 90% of countries). This indicates that stacking-based ensemble approaches can improve the accuracy and stability of cross-country achievement prediction, supporting more reliable identification of underperforming students for targeted instructional interventions, though the study’s missing-data and weighting procedures are not fully specified for causal interpretation.

main_findings.target_variable: Reading achievement prediction error (MAPE/MAE/MSE/RMSE across PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Stacking produced the lowest mean MAPE for 64/80 countries (80.00%), lowest mean MAE for 69/80 (86.25%), and lowest mean MSE for 70/80 (87.50%). Robust linear mixed-effects models (reference=Stacking) indicated significantly higher MAPE/MAE/MSE for XGBoost, HGB, LightGBM, and Blending vs. Stacking (e.g., MAPE: XGBoost t=10.60, HGB t=12.86, LightGBM t=11.00, Blending t=21.25).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Reading the study leveraged an ensemble stacking meta-model (ridge regression at level 1) to predict reading achievement across plausible values, finding that stacking delivered the lowest mean prediction errors in most countries (e.g., lowest mean MAPE in 80% of countries). This indicates that stacking can provide more accurate and robust predictive performance for reading outcomes across diverse education systems, which may help policymakers and schools prioritize reading support strategies, while the reported results remain predictive (not causal) and depend on the study’s unspecified handling of missingness and survey design.

main_findings.target_variable: Science achievement prediction error (MAPE/MAE/MSE/RMSE across PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Stacking produced the lowest mean MAPE for 65/80 countries (81.25%), lowest mean MAE for 71/80 (88.75%), and lowest mean MSE for 71/80 (88.75%). Robust linear mixed-effects models (reference=Stacking) indicated significantly higher MAPE/MAE/MSE for XGBoost, HGB, LightGBM, and Blending vs. Stacking (e.g., MAPE: XGBoost t=11.51, HGB t=11.95, LightGBM t=10.74, Blending t=20.00).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Science the study leveraged an ensemble stacking meta-model (ridge regression as the level-1 learner) to predict science achievement across plausible values, finding that stacking achieved the lowest error metrics for the majority of countries (e.g., lowest mean MAPE in 81.25% of countries). This indicates that stacking-based ensembles may be a strong option for improving predictive accuracy of science performance in large-scale assessments, enabling more dependable targeting of science learning interventions, while causality cannot be inferred and reproducibility is limited by incomplete reporting of missing-data and weighting decisions.

data.outcome_summary: The study predicts PISA 2022 student achievement in mathematics, reading, and science for 80 participating countries using ensemble machine learning. For each subject, the authors build level-0 base learners (XGBoost, HGB, LightGBM) and combine their predictions with a ridge-regression meta-learner in a stacking framework; blending is evaluated using a validation-based input strategy. Missing values are converted to NaN during preparation, and the authors state that they do not impute missing observations, but they do not fully specify whether rows are deleted or how missingness is handled internally by each learner. Model performance is evaluated with MAPE, MAE, MSE, and RMSE computed across 10 plausible values per subject, and robust linear mixed-effects models (countries as random effects) test algorithm differences. Across subjects, stacking most often yields the lowest mean errors (e.g., lowest mean MAPE in 90% of countries for mathematics), indicating improved predictive accuracy and stability, though the study’s survey-weighting and missing-data procedures are not transparently documented for design-based inference.
